doc.title: Dave Brubeck — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Practising at Mills and developing voicings by ear
summary: He did no scales or Hannon, improvised and altered songs, and found his chord voicings by ear; Milhaud once showed him a huge polytonal chart.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Let’s go back to the time at Mills College, how you learned and studied then. What was your practice regimen then? How did you practice the piano? What did you do during those years or before to develop? Did you play though scales and Hannon? Or did you just improvise? What would you do?
Nothing that [ ] classical good pianist. Today I do Hannon once in a while, but I never bothered when I should have, when I was young, to help get some fingers more quickly.
Did you do any scales back then, Cherney, or any of these exercises?
What would you do when you were sitting at the piano by yourself after classes? You would just play songs? Would you compose? Would you improvise?
Improvise, and play songs, and alter them – take off.
How did you develop your chord voicings? Did someone teach you those? Did you do them by ear?

Mostly by ear. Milhaud one time showed me a chart that he developed for polytonal chords. You can’t remember something that somebody just said, “Look at this.” So I wasn’t – what I was aware of, that he’d probably tried every possible tonality. The chart was so big – pages.
No, I wouldn’t have brains enough to study off of it.
So basically, you’ve got – your sense of harmony was really unique in jazz at the time you were doing these things. So really, you were doing these by ear.
You were working through combinations of notes at the keyboard, trying to hear what sounded right to you, and you would bring those to the gig.
